title: Hideki Tojo
subtitle: The general who led Japan into war with America

package.intro: Hideki Tojo was Japan's prime minister when it attacked Pearl Harbor in December 1941. After the war he was tried in Tokyo, convicted of waging aggressive war and of permitting atrocities against prisoners, and hanged. This documentary tells his story and asks how much of Japan's war was really his.
facts: Chief of staff of the Kwantung Army in Manchuria from 1937
Became minister of war in July 1940; Japan signed the Tripartite Pact on 27 September 1940
Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941, killing more than 2,400 Americans
According to the Tokyo tribunal, about 27% of Western prisoners held by Japan died, against about 4% held by Germany and Italy
Resigned on 18 July 1944 after the fall of Saipan
Survived a suicide attempt on 11 September 1945
Convicted by the International Military Tribunal for the Far East on 12 November 1948 and hanged on 23 December 1948
package.sources: Judgment of the International Military Tribunal for the Far East (1948), Encyclopaedia Britannica, National WWII Museum (New Orleans), Herbert P. Bix's Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan, John W. Dower's Embracing Defeat, Rana Mitter's China's War with Japan.

sections.name: Cold open

lines.title: HIDEKI TOJO
lines.sub: The general who led Japan into war with America

lines: On the eleventh of September 1945, American military police arrived at a house in a Tokyo suburb. The man inside was Japan's wartime prime minister. As they came to the door, he shot himself in the chest.
He survived. American doctors treated him, and he was nursed back to health so that he could stand trial.
The war he had helped lead killed around three million Japanese, and many millions more across Asia and the Pacific.
To Americans, Hideki Tojo became the face of Japanese militarism. But he was not a dictator like Hitler, and his story raises a hard question about who was really responsible.

sections.name: The Razor
lines: Hideki Tojo was born in Tokyo on the thirtieth of December 1884. His father was an army officer who rose to become a general.

Japan was turning itself, at astonishing speed, into a modern industrial power, with an army and navy built on European lines. In 1905, the year Tojo graduated from the military academy, Japan defeated Russia in war.

lines.name: Hideki Tojo
lines.role: Army officer. Tireless, rigid, efficient. Nicknamed 'the Razor'.

lines: He was not brilliant, but he was tireless, rigid and efficient. Colleagues nicknamed him the Razor. After the First World War, he served as an officer in Switzerland and Germany.
Back home, he joined the army's Control faction, which wanted the whole nation organised for total war. When rival officers attempted a coup in February 1936 and failed, his faction's power grew.

sections.name: War in China
lines: In 1931, Japanese officers in Manchuria, in north-east China, staged a bombing on a railway and used it as an excuse to seize the whole region. It became a puppet state called Manchukuo.
Tojo was sent there in 1935 to command the military police of the Kwantung Army, Japan's force in Manchuria. In 1937 he became its chief of staff.

In July 1937, a clash near Beijing became a full-scale war with China. That December, Japanese troops captured the Chinese capital, Nanjing, and carried out a massacre. Estimates of the dead range from tens of thousands to three hundred thousand.
In China alone, historians estimate that the war killed somewhere between ten and twenty million people.

sections.name: Minister of war
lines: In July 1940, Tojo became minister of war. Two months later, Japan signed the Tripartite Pact, allying itself with Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy.

lines.text: Do not live to suffer the shame of being taken prisoner.
lines.who: Field Service Code, issued under War Minister Tojo · 1941 (translation)

lines: In January 1941, his ministry issued a code of conduct for soldiers. Its most famous line told them never to suffer the shame of being taken prisoner. Many soldiers later fought to the death, or killed themselves, rather than surrender.
In 1940 and 1941, Japanese troops moved into French Indochina, closer to the oil and rubber of South-East Asia.
The United States responded by freezing Japanese assets and cutting off oil. Most of Japan's oil came from America.

The prime minister, Prince Konoe, wanted a deal. America's price included withdrawal from China. Tojo refused, arguing that the army could not abandon what its soldiers had died for. Konoe's government fell.

sections.name: Pearl Harbor
lines: On the eighteenth of October 1941, Tojo became prime minister, while remaining minister of war. The emperor's closest adviser had recommended him, hoping he could keep the army under control.
Talks with Washington went nowhere. At a conference held in the emperor's presence on the first of December, Japan's leaders formally decided on war.

On the seventh of December 1941, Japanese carrier planes attacked the American fleet at Pearl Harbor, in Hawaii. More than two thousand four hundred Americans were killed. Within hours, Japan struck British and American territory across Asia.
For six months, Japan swept across Asia: Hong Kong, Malaya, Singapore, the Dutch East Indies, the Philippines and Burma.

lines.name: Prime Minister Tojo
lines.role: Prime minister and war minister. Later also army chief of staff.

lines: He piled up posts. Alongside being prime minister and war minister, he also, at different times, ran the home ministry, the munitions ministry and the army general staff.
At home, he was the public face of the war. Political parties had been merged into a single patriotic association, and the military police watched for dissent.

sections.name: Prisoners
lines: Japan's treatment of prisoners was among the worst of the war. According to figures presented at the Tokyo war crimes trial, about twenty-seven percent of Western prisoners held by Japan died in captivity.
That compared with about four percent of Western prisoners held by Germany and Italy.
In the Philippines in April 1942, captured American and Filipino soldiers were forced to march for days in the heat. Thousands died on what became known as the Bataan Death March.
On the railway built between Burma and Thailand, about twelve thousand Allied prisoners died, along with tens of thousands of Asian labourers.
Across occupied Asia, the Japanese military massacred civilians, used forced labour, forced tens of thousands of women into sexual slavery, and carried out lethal experiments on prisoners.

sections.name: Defeat
lines: The tide turned at the Battle of Midway in June 1942, when Japan lost four aircraft carriers. After that, American forces advanced island by island.
In July 1944, the island of Saipan fell, putting Japan's cities in range of American bombers. Tojo was forced to resign.
In March 1945, a single American firebombing raid on Tokyo killed around a hundred thousand people. In August, atomic bombs destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
On the fifteenth of August, Emperor Hirohito announced Japan's surrender on the radio. For most Japanese, it was the first time they had heard his voice.

sections.name: The Tokyo trial

lines.label: International Military Tribunal for the Far East · Tokyo · 1946 – 1948

lines: In 1946, Tojo and twenty-seven other leaders went on trial before an international tribunal in Tokyo, with judges from eleven countries.

lines.name: Emperor Hirohito
lines.role: Emperor of Japan from 1926. Never put on trial.

lines: One man was not in the dock. The American occupation, led by General Douglas MacArthur, had decided that Emperor Hirohito would not be tried, to help keep Japan stable.

lines.text: He took responsibility for the war, but called it self-defence.

lines: Tojo accepted responsibility for the war, but insisted it had been fought in self-defence. When he once implied that no Japanese would act against the emperor's will, he soon revised his testimony, helping to keep the emperor out of the case.
In November 1948, he was convicted of waging wars of aggression and of permitting the inhumane treatment of prisoners of war. He was one of seven men sentenced to death.
He was hanged at Sugamo Prison in Tokyo on the twenty-third of December 1948. He was sixty-three.

sections.name: Legacy
lines: The trial still divides opinion. One judge, Radhabinod Pal of India, would have acquitted every defendant, arguing that the court was imposing victors' justice.
Historians also stress that Japan was not run by one man. The navy planned Pearl Harbor, the emperor approved the war, and many officials shared the decisions. Tojo was powerful, but never absolute.

In 1978, Tojo and thirteen other convicted wartime leaders were secretly enshrined at Yasukuni, a Tokyo shrine to Japan's war dead. Visits there by Japanese politicians still anger China and South Korea.
Tojo's name has become shorthand for Japan's war. That is partly fair. He pushed for war, and he presided over its crimes.
But the lesson of his story is bigger than one man. A war of conquest needs many willing hands, and every one of them shares the blame.
